title: Two Capitals, Two Powers
bullets: For four hundred years Japan kept its sacred emperor in Kyoto and gave the real power away to a warrior caste — two capitals, two powers, one country.

The emperor claimed descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu and was treated as a sacred axle the realm turned on, leaving real authority to Fujiwara regents and, through the insei system, to retired emperors ruling from their cloisters.
The Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 pitted the Taira clan, who under Taira no Kiyomori had clawed into the court itself, against their bitter rivals the Minamoto.
The war ended in 1185 at the sea battle of Dan-no-ura, where Minamoto no Yoshitsune's fleet destroyed the Taira navy and the child-emperor Antoku drowned with them.
Minamoto no Yoritomo won the country and did the opposite of what an ambitious general should — he refused the throne, stayed in the east, and built a second government at Kamakura.
From 1185 Yoritomo planted his power in the provinces through two new offices, the shugo military governors and the jitō land stewards, all answering to Kamakura rather than the court.
His regime was the bakufu, literally 'tent government,' and in 1192 the court granted him the title sei-i taishōgun — shogun — the supreme general who actually ran Japan in the emperor's name.

Yoritomo turned on Yoshitsune, the brother who had won the war, and hunted him to suicide in 1189 — the first instance of a pattern in which the man who wins the war becomes the new order's greatest threat.
Almost everything vivid known about the war comes from the sung epic the Tale of the Heike, polished into national myth, set against the winners' own flattering chronicle, the Azuma Kagami.

title: The Power Behind the Power
bullets: After Yoritomo died in 1199, real power slid to the family he had married into — the Hōjō — who ruled through puppet shoguns without ever taking the title themselves.
Hōjō Masako, Yoritomo's formidable widow, became the 'nun shogun' (ama-shōgun) and held the regime together through its early crises.
The Hōjō invented the office of shikken, nominally 'regent' but in practice the actual ruler of Japan, passing real power from Hōjō father to Hōjō son for over a century.
When the puppet shogun Sanetomo was assassinated in 1219, the Minamoto main line went extinct, and the Hōjō imported an infant of noble Kyoto blood to be a figurehead shogun.
In 1221 the retired emperor Go-Toba launched the Jōkyū War to destroy Kamakura, betting the warriors would rally to the throne — and lost completely.

Kamakura took Kyoto within a month, exiled three retired emperors including Go-Toba, and confiscated some three thousand rebel estates, proving the sacred throne could be overruled by men with swords.
In 1232 the regent Hōjō Yasutoki issued the Jōei Code, the first law code written by and for warriors — a practical handbook for land disputes that became the foundation of warrior law for centuries.
Land was held as shōen, private estates layered with overlapping rights, so an honest court that judged land claims fairly was worth more to a warrior than almost anything.
Historians describe the period as a kenmon system — court, religious institutions, and warrior government sharing power and checking one another.

The Kamakura warrior followed the rough 'way of the bow and horse,' not the later philosophical bushidō, and out of these wars hardened the practice of seppuku, ritual suicide over the dishonor of capture.

title: A New Religion for a New Age
bullets: The Kamakura new Buddhism blew open a faith that had been an elaborate, scholarly, monastery-bound affair and handed religion to the common people for the first time.
The monk Hōnen, from around 1175, taught Pure Land Buddhism: salvation by sincerely reciting the nembutsu, the formula 'Namu Amida Butsu,' with trust in the Buddha Amida's vow.

Hōnen's disciple Shinran founded True Pure Land Buddhism around 1224, teaching that salvation came entirely from Amida's grace — a move that rhymed with Martin Luther's faith-alone doctrine three centuries before Luther.
Nichiren, from around 1253, built a fierce movement on the Lotus Sutra, denounced every rival school, and warned of a foreign invasion that would soon arrive and vindicate him.
Zen reached Japan from China in this period in two forms: Eisai's Rinzai school, with its baffling kōan riddles, and Dōgen's Sōtō school of 'just sitting' meditation, centered at Eihei-ji.
The warrior class embraced Zen because its self-control, disdain for book-learning, and direct confrontation of death fit men whose trade was death; the Hōjō regents became its great patrons.
Eisai brought back tea seeds along with Rinzai Zen in 1191, introducing matcha as a stimulant to keep monks awake — the small monastic beginning of what would become the tea ceremony.
The sculptor Unkei carved the colossal, snarling Niō guardian kings at Nara in a new muscular realism that broke with the serene court style.
Around 1252 Kamakura cast the Great Buddha (Daibutsu), a forty-foot bronze Amida that still sits in the open air after its hall was swept away by storm and wave.

title: The Divine Wind
bullets: In 1268 Kublai Khan, ruler of the largest land empire in history, sent Japan a demand to submit — the opening move of the only foreign invasion the Asian mainland ever threw at Japan.
The Hōjō regent Hōjō Tokimune refused, eventually beheading Kublai's envoys, and ordered the warriors of Kyushu to prepare for war.
The first invasion landed at Hakata Bay in 1274; the Mongols' disciplined mass formations, volley fire, and exploding bombs shocked samurai raised on individual mounted combat.
The Mongols withdrew after one day's fighting and a storm wrecked part of their fleet — though historians doubt this first 'storm' and suspect a calculated withdrawal exaggerated by legend.
From 1276 the Japanese built a stone-and-earth defensive wall around Hakata Bay to deny the enemy the open beach where their formations were deadliest.
The second invasion of 1281 came in two enormous fleets carrying perhaps 140,000 men, but the wall and a stubborn defense penned the army offshore for weeks.
A well-attested typhoon caught the fleet at anchor in late summer 1281 and smashed it, drowning much of the army — and Japan was never invaded from the mainland again.
The Japanese named the storms kamikaze, the 'divine wind,' breeding a belief in supernatural immunity to invasion that resurfaced darkly in the suicide pilots of 1945.
The samurai Takezaki Suenaga commissioned an illustrated scroll of his deeds around 1293, not from pride but as evidence to press his claim for a reward.

The victory produced no conquered land to hand out, so the reward crisis hollowed out the regime; the 1297 Einin Debt Cancellation Edict relieved indebted warriors but wrecked the credit system and the shogunate's credibility.

title: The Emperor Who Wanted It All
bullets: Emperor Go-Daigo, enthroned in 1318 already a grown man, refused to be a scheduled ornament and set out to destroy the Kamakura shogunate and rule directly.
The picture of his age comes through the sprawling, semi-fictional war chronicle the Taiheiki, gorgeous literature that invents speeches and sharpens heroes into saints.
Go-Daigo's plots leaked twice; after the second, in 1331, the Hōjō exiled the reigning emperor of Japan to the remote Oki Islands.
He escaped in 1333 and raised his standard again, drawing the support of a minor warrior named Kusunoki Masashige, who tied down huge Hōjō armies with mountain-fortress guerrilla warfare at Chihaya.
The great eastern lord Ashikaga Takauji, sent to crush the rebellion, switched sides in 1333 and captured Kyoto for the emperor instead.
Nitta Yoshisada marched on Kamakura itself and broke in; the last Hōjō regent and several hundred clansmen killed themselves, ending 148 years of Kamakura rule.

Go-Daigo's Kemmu Restoration tried to abolish the warrior government and rule directly, but collapsed in three years under administrative paralysis, money troubles, and his failure to reward the warriors who won his throne.
Above all he refused to make Takauji shogun, leaving the most dangerous man in Japan ambitious and slighted; Takauji broke with him in 1336.

Ordered by court nobles into a hopeless head-on battle at Minatogawa, Kusunoki Masashige obeyed and died in 1336 — loyalty unto a death he knew was pointless, the model warrior Japan later venerated above all.
Takauji took Kyoto and installed a rival emperor; Go-Daigo fled to the mountains of Yoshino and declared himself the true sovereign, leaving Japan with two emperors at once.

title: Two Emperors, One Throne
bullets: From 1336 to 1392 — the Nanboku-chō era — Japan had two rival emperors: Takauji's Northern Court in Kyoto and Go-Daigo's Southern Court in the mountains of Yoshino.
The war dragged on for half a century because the two courts gave every ambitious warrior a choice of masters, turning loyalty into a permanent auction for land and rank.
In 1338 the Northern emperor granted Takauji the title of shogun, founding the Ashikaga shogunate, also called the Muromachi shogunate after its Kyoto district.
Takauji set his government in the capital itself rather than far to the east — a choice that made it cultured and courtly but gradually disconnected it from the provinces.
In 1339 the Southern loyalist Kitabatake Chikafusa wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki, arguing Japan was a divine land ruled in an unbroken sacred line — an idea quoted by nationalists six hundred years later.
The monk Musō Soseki fused Zen to Ashikaga power and helped organize the leading Zen temples into the ranked Gozan network that served as the era's universities, bankers, and diplomatic corps.
The Ashikaga funded grand projects on the China trade, sending the Tenryū-ji ships to China in 1342 to raise money for a temple built to pray for the dead Go-Daigo.
The provincial military governors, the shugo, mutated into hereditary regional warlords — the shugo-daimyō — the larval stage of the later Sengoku lords.
Bands of sea-raiders called the wakō plundered the coasts of Korea and China, a chronic problem the shogunate could not police.
The third shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, broke the over-mighty shugo and in 1392 reunited the Northern and Southern Courts, giving Japan a single emperor again.

title: The Golden Pavilion
bullets: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the third shogun, was the closest thing medieval Japan produced to an absolute monarch — and the high-water mark of warrior government, strong, solvent, and culturally radiant at once.
He climbed the imperial court's own ranks to the office of grand chancellor, outranking nearly everyone and treating the emperor almost as a junior partner.
In 1397 he began building the Golden Pavilion, the Kinkaku-ji, its top two stories sheathed in gold leaf, blending court, warrior, and Zen architectural styles into one building.
In 1404 Yoshimitsu accepted the title 'King of Japan' from the Ming emperor — formally a vassal's status — to win the lucrative tally trade.
The licensed tally trade used the kangō, paper tallies that distinguished sanctioned Japanese merchants from the wakō pirates plaguing the China coast.
Because the shogun was not the sacred emperor, he could stomach the humiliation of subordination to China for the sake of copper coins and silk that the emperor never could have.
The China trade poured Chinese goods and ideas into Kyoto and rooted monochrome ink-wash landscape painting in Japan, filtered through the Gozan Zen temples.
Yoshimitsu's patronage transformed the rough village variety show called sarugaku into Noh theater, after the actor Kan'ami performed before him in the 1370s.

Kan'ami's son Zeami perfected Noh and wrote treatises on its aesthetics centered on yūgen, subtle mysterious beauty — making it the oldest major theater tradition still performed in near-original form.
When Yoshimitsu died in 1408 the machinery he had mastered began to come apart, and no Ashikaga shogun after him was ever so powerful.

title: Tea, Ink, and Emptiness
bullets: The arts the world thinks of as the essence of Japanese taste flowered at the very moment the government fell apart — under the same man, on a rotting branch.
The eighth shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimasa, was a man of exquisite taste and no aptitude for governing, who retreated into art while his regime drifted and rotted.
His predecessor the sixth shogun was murdered at a banquet by a vassal in 1441, exposing how hollow shogunal authority had become.
Villagers bound into leagues called ikki repeatedly marched on Kyoto demanding tokusei, debt-cancellation decrees, draining power from the center at the bottom as well as the top.
Yoshimasa built the Silver Pavilion, the Ginkaku-ji, which despite its name was never covered in silver — bare weathered wood that became the perfect emblem of the new restrained aesthetic.
The Higashiyama culture prized restraint, asymmetry, and refined poverty of means, crystallizing the taste the world came to recognize as quintessentially Japanese.
The tea adviser Murata Jukō turned tea away from show-off parties toward wabi — the beauty of the plain, worn, and humble — the spiritual root of the full tea ceremony.
The painter-monk Sesshū Tōyō traveled to Ming China and brought ink-wash painting to its Japanese summit with bold, sharply structured brushwork.
The Zen temples developed the karesansui dry-landscape garden of raked gravel and placed rocks, most famously at Ryōan-ji, built to be contemplated rather than entered.
The reclusive monk Yoshida Kenkō's earlier Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa) captured the era's mood: that things are beautiful because they do not last.

title: The Capital Burns
bullets: The Ōnin War ran ten years, burned the most beautiful city in the country, and decided almost nothing — except that no one was in charge of Japan anymore.
The Ashikaga ruled the provinces only through the shugo military governors, who had turned their offices into hereditary domains; the shogun balanced on the great houses rather than commanding them.
In the 1441 Kakitsu Incident the sixth shogun, Ashikaga Yoshinori, was assassinated at a banquet by the lord Akamatsu Mitsusuke, shattering the office's aura of untouchability.
Debt-cancellation uprisings by village ikki demanding tokusei hit Kyoto again and again, the crowds storming pawnshops and burning loan records.
The childless eighth shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa named his brother Yoshimi heir in 1464, then had a son, Yoshihisa, in 1465 — setting up a ruinous succession dispute.
Two great lords lined up on opposite sides: Hosokawa Katsumoto, the kanrei, against Yamana Sōzen, the 'Red Monk' and his own father-in-law.
By 1467 some hundred thousand troops were camped in Kyoto; the Hosokawa Eastern Army and Yamana Western Army turned the wooden city into a fortified battlefield.
Kyoto burned — whole districts, temples, libraries, and the records of the oldest noble families lost, gutting the physical core of classical Japanese civilization.
Both principals died of illness in 1473 with the war unwon, and from 1477 the armies simply went home to defend provinces being stolen behind their backs.
The war revealed the office of shogun to be empty and opened the Sengoku, the Warring States century, conventionally dated from 1467.

title: A Country of Warlords
bullets: After the armies left Kyoto in 1477 there was a sacred broke emperor and a powerless shogun, but the structure of command reaching into the provinces was gone for a century.
The age ran on gekokujō, 'the low overthrowing the high' — retainers murdering lords, deputies shoving aside governors, men of no birth ruling provinces.
Hōjō Sōun, often called the first true Sengoku daimyō, rose from a modest position to control Odawara and the rich Kantō plain, founding the Later Hōjō.
The new lords wrote their own domain law codes, the bunkokuhō, each a little legal system for one warlord's territory, often binding the lord himself to his own rules.
The signature settlement was the castle town, the jōkamachi, gathering warriors, artisans, and merchants under the castle walls — a tool to pry the warrior class off the land.
The merchant port of Sakai governed itself through a council of leading merchants, defended by its own moat and militia, an island of self-rule compared to Venice.
The Ikkō-ikki, armed leagues of True Pure Land Buddhists, rose in Kaga province in 1488, drove the shugo to suicide, and ran the province as a 'province held by peasants' for nearly a century.
The Iwami silver mine, opened from the 1520s and 1530s, turned Japan into one of the great silver producers of the world, funding armies, foreign guns, and global trade.
The decisive new force on the battlefield was the ashigaru, the mass-recruited commoner foot soldier, who in disciplined blocks made the elite mounted archer obsolete.

title: Tigers and Dragons
bullets: The high Sengoku of the mid-sixteenth century is the romantic peak of the samurai age — and the moment just before guns and mass armies made all of it obsolete.
A lord's power was measured in koku, the amount of rice to feed one person for a year; the banners and codes of honor all sat on an account book in bushels of rice.

Takeda Shingen, the 'Tiger of Kai,' was the complete daimyō — fierce commander, shrewd administrator, master of feared cavalry — whose banner carried the Sun Tzu motto 'swift as the wind, silent as the forest, fierce as the fire, immovable as the mountain.'
Uesugi Kenshin, the 'Dragon' of Echigo, was Shingen's devout rival; the two fought five times at Kawanakajima between 1553 and 1564 without either destroying the other.
The most famous Kawanakajima episode — Kenshin attacking Shingen personally, the seated lord parrying with his war fan — is likely a later invention storytellers loved to add.
Mōri Motonari rose from a single small domain to dominate western Honshu and is remembered for the parable of the three arrows bound together that none could break.
Date Masamune, the one-eyed dragon of the northeast, carved out a huge domain late in the Sengoku and in 1613 sent an embassy across the Pacific to Mexico, Spain, and the Pope in Rome.
The katana reached its peak through folding, hammering, and differential hardening, but on the actual battlefield the sword was a sidearm and much of its mystique was elaborated later.
Seppuku had hardened into the supreme proof of warrior honor, though the polished philosophy of bushidō was largely a later, peacetime creation.
The ninja had a real kernel in the spies and saboteurs of the Iga and Kōga regions, and armed warrior-monks, the sōhei, fielded their own troops and fortified temple-complexes.

title: The Black Ships and the Demon King
bullets: Oda Nobunaga inherited a minor domain in Owari around 1551 and was so widely dismissed as a half-wit that he was nicknamed 'the great fool of Owari' — but he was a different kind of animal entirely.

In 1543 Portuguese aboard a storm-blown junk landed on Tanegashima carrying the matchlock musket; Japanese smiths copied it and within a generation made the country one of the most gun-saturated on earth.
Francis Xavier, a Jesuit priest, came ashore in 1549 and seeded a mission that converted hundreds of thousands, including a handful of Christian daimyō.
Missionaries and merchants arrived on the same black ships — the Nanban trade — so a daimyō who welcomed the priests was courting Portuguese guns, silk, and silver.

In 1560 at Okehazama, the hopelessly outnumbered Nobunaga used a sudden thunderstorm to fall on the camped army of Imagawa Yoshimoto and killed him, becoming a man the whole country had to take seriously.
Among the lords freed by Imagawa's death was Tokugawa Ieyasu, who became Nobunaga's loyal ally — the steadiest relationship of his violent life.
Nobunaga marched into Kyoto in 1568 and installed Ashikaga Yoshiaki as a puppet shogun, then expelled him in 1573, formally ending the Ashikaga shogunate.

In 1571 Nobunaga burned the seven-centuries-old temple-fortress of Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei to the ground, killing thousands and breaking the political power of the great monasteries — earning the name Demon King.
At Nagashino in 1575 his matchlock-armed ashigaru behind palisades destroyed the feared Takeda cavalry, demonstrating that massed firepower had finished the mounted samurai archer.
In 1582, near to ruling all Japan, Nobunaga was betrayed by his own general Akechi Mitsuhide and died in the burning temple of Honnō-ji — gekokujō in its purest distilled form.

title: The Peasant Who Ruled Japan
bullets: Hearing of Nobunaga's death in 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi made peace with his own enemy, raced his army back, and crushed the murderer Mitsuhide at Yamazaki within about eleven days.

Born a peasant around 1537 and entering Nobunaga's service as a sandal-bearer, Hideyoshi rose purely on ability — the most extraordinary social ascent in Japanese history and gekokujō at its logical extreme.
He finished the unification by mixing war with diplomacy, and in 1590 surrounded the last great holdout, the Later Hōjō at Odawara, ending the Sengoku for the first unified Japan since 1467.
Barred from the title of shogun by his peasant birth, Hideyoshi had himself appointed kampaku, imperial regent, after being adopted into a great noble family.
His tea master Sen no Rikyū perfected wabi-cha, shrinking the tea room and developing rustic raku ware — and tea was politics, the room where deals were struck.
In 1591 Hideyoshi ordered Rikyū, the most revered cultural figure of the age, to commit seppuku, for reasons still debated.
The 1588 sword hunt confiscated weapons from farmers and commoners, making the sword the privilege of the samurai alone and drawing a hard line between warrior and everyone else.

The land survey registered every rice field in koku and, with edicts forbidding people to change occupation, froze Japanese society into rigid hereditary classes — Hideyoshi pulling up the ladder he had climbed.
From 1592 he launched the catastrophic invasions of Korea (the Imjin War), broken by Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships, guerrilla resistance, and Ming Chinese intervention.
In 1597 he had the Twenty-Six Martyrs crucified at Nagasaki, and he died in 1598 with his armies still bleeding in Korea and his heir, Toyotomi Hideyori, only five years old.

title: The Gambler's Victory
bullets: Tokugawa Ieyasu was the third great unifier and, above all, a survivor — the 'waiter' who outlasted Nobunaga the breaker and Hideyoshi the builder.
A saying captures the three: confronted with a bird that will not sing, Nobunaga says 'kill it,' Hideyoshi says 'make it want to sing,' and Ieyasu says 'wait.'

After Hideyoshi died in 1598, Japan was to be governed by a council of Five Elders sworn to protect the boy Hideyori, but Ieyasu, the most powerful of them, began building his own faction from his eastern base at Edo.
His chief opponent, the administrator Ishida Mitsunari, rallied the lords still loyal to the Toyotomi house, and by 1600 Japan had split into an Eastern Army and a Western Army.
The two armies, around eighty thousand men each, met at Sekigahara in October 1600 — possibly the largest and most consequential battle ever fought on Japanese soil.

The battle turned on treachery arranged in advance: around midday Kobayakawa Hideaki led his force down from the hills and charged into the flank of the Western Army he was supposed to be fighting for.
The betrayal cascaded, the Western Army collapsed within hours, and Mitsunari was captured and executed — the gambler's victory of a patient man who had fixed the odds beforehand.
In 1603 the emperor named Ieyasu shogun, a title his plausible Minamoto lineage allowed; he built his government far from Kyoto at Edo, exactly as Yoritomo had done at Kamakura in 1185.
This founded the Tokugawa shogunate, the third and most durable warrior government, ending the medieval age on the same kind of act that opened it.

The great white castle of Himeji, the 'White Heron,' marked the age's architectural peak, while the Tokugawa sealed Japan shut — suppressing Christianity and reducing European contact to the Dutch post at Dejima — and the polished myth of bushidō was assembled in the long peace that followed.
